clue.text: In Mexico her extremists stick together

indicators.note: 'In' says the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: Two Mexican women at the far ends of politics form a pact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' looks like the political sense, but it only supplies its first letter to finish the run across 'Mexico her e-'.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that hold firmly together, physically or logically, are said to cohere.

clue.text: Be a model of anything

parts.note: to be the perfect example or emblem of something, standing for the whole of its kind

explanation.definitionFit: To serve as the characteristic example of a thing is to embody its type.

clue.text: Judas's price plucked from some thick old head?

definitions.text: plucked from some thick old head?

explanation.surface: A betrayer's fee compared with tufts pulled from an aged scalp.
explanation.walkthrough: Judas was paid thirty pieces of silver for betraying Jesus; the second reading takes silver as grey hair, a fistful tugged from a thick-haired old head.
explanation.definitionFit: Judas's reward was a quantity of silver coins; a fistful of grey hair is the playful second sense.

clue.text: 4 A dealer in corsages, bloomers, etc…

definitions.text: A dealer in corsages, bloomers, etc

parts.words: A dealer in corsages, bloomers, etc
parts.note: bloomers suggests underwear and corsages bodices, but both are really flowers, so this is a seller of blooms

explanation.walkthrough: Corsages and bloomers sound like lingerie, yet a corsage is a spray of flowers and a bloomer is a plant in flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopkeeper selling cut flowers and floral arrangements is the trade in question.

clue.text: Here a push-button start C should bring the motorist to a halt

definitions.text: Here a push-button start C should bring the motorist to a halt

parts.words: Here a push-button start C should bring the motorist to a halt
parts.note: describes a road crossing where a walker presses a button and the lights stop the traffic

explanation.walkthrough: A PELICAN CROSSING is the British pedestrian crossing with push-button traffic lights; the name comes from 'pedestrian light controlled'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestrian-operated signal crossing stops cars when someone on foot presses its button.

clue.text: Trial before shooting?

parts.note: shooting means filming with a camera, not firing a gun, so this is an audition on camera

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shooting' suggests an execution after a trial; in the cinema it means filming.
explanation.definitionFit: A screen audition is a trial an actor undergoes before a film is shot.

clue.text: Delay mail 1p over

parts.note: to post is to send mail

indicators.note: over means the penny's letter is turned over to the front of the one

parts.note: 1p is one penny, spelt ONE then P

explanation.surface: An instruction to hold back a letter with a penny's postage too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' carries P from the end of ONEP round to the front, giving PONE after POST.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something off until later is to delay it.

clue.text: A tip only possible for a little horse

definitions.text: A tip only possible for a little horse

indicators.note: possible signals one feasible rearrangement of the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A tipster offering a racing tip that suits only a pony.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail is the tip of a little horse, and the letters of 'A tip only' rearranged give the hairstyle named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pony's tail is literally the tip of a small horse, and the hairstyle borrows its name.

clue.text: Leader of a press gang?

parts.note: a press gang forced men into the navy, but here the press is newspapers and the gang its staff

explanation.walkthrough: A press gang once kidnapped sailors for the Royal Navy; read as 'the press' plus a gang, its boss runs a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The person in charge of a newspaper's journalists heads the team that produces the paper.

clue.text: Awfully low night flier

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the three letters that follow are jumbled

explanation.surface: A bird flying very low after dark.
explanation.definitionFit: This bird hunts at night and is the classic nocturnal flying creature.

clue.text: A jogger, and won't let you forget it

explanation.surface: A runner who keeps reminding you of the fact.
explanation.walkthrough: A jogger here is something that jogs the memory, not a runner.
explanation.definitionFit: A prompt or note jogs your memory and makes sure you do not overlook something.

clue.text: One who lives in a central station in decrepit mine

indicators.note: the A and the station's middle letter go inside the jumbled word
decrepit means broken down, so the letters of mine are reworked
central picks out the middle letter of station

explanation.surface: Someone living in an old station building in a run-down mining town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decrepit' turns MINE into INME, and 'central' takes T, the middle of 'station'; A and T go inside, between INM and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident of a prison or institution is one who lives within it.

clue.text: Hasten to do so if you want to cut a fine figure

definitions.text: to do so if you want to cut a fine figure

explanation.surface: Advice to hurry if you want to look good.
explanation.walkthrough: The everyday idiom means hurry up; literally, you must put skates on to cut a figure on the ice.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom urges speed, and figure skating requires wearing skates.

clue.text: The couple coming before three

explanation.surface: A pair arriving ahead of a third party.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple is a pair, and in counting that number precedes three.

clue.text: He has developed views highly thought of in Wales

explanation.surface: A man whose opinions have matured, much admired by the Welsh.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Snowdon was a noted photographer who developed pictures; Snowdon is also the highest mountain in Wales, so 'highly' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The photographer Earl of Snowdon printed photographs, and the Welsh peak stands highest in that country.

clue.text: The actor should be learning the following section

explanation.surface: An actor must study the next passage of the script.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor learns the role to come, and the subsequent portion of anything is what comes after.

clue.text: Barges in where ringleader is manoeuvring

indicators.note: manoeuvring means moving about, so the combined letters are shifted into a new order

parts.note: the leader of ring is its first letter

explanation.surface: A boat pushes in where the gang boss is plotting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barges in' reads as a verb phrase; 'Barges' is the plural noun and 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: These are light rowing boats or barges once used to carry goods and passengers on rivers.

clue.text: Mown down by a Father who never stops?

definitions.text: Mown down by a Father who never stops?

parts.words: Mown down by a Father who never stops?
parts.note: Father Time carries a long curved blade and never stops, so cut down by him with that blade

explanation.walkthrough: Father Time is pictured as an old man with a scythe; time never stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutting grass or crops with a long curved blade is mowing, the tool Father Time carries.

clue.text: He takes half of us in colour

indicators.note: takes means the first word holds the next piece within it
half of picks the first of the two letters of us

explanation.surface: A man who takes his share of what we have in paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A shade or tint is another word for a colour.

clue.text: How we imagine our earliest days

explanation.surface: Thinking back to childhood in imagination.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN FANCY, the answer means 'in imagination'; whole, it is the first stage of life.
explanation.definitionFit: Fancy is imagination, and babyhood is the earliest period of life.

clue.text: Excitedly expect Jones? Be no counter of the cost, of course!

definitions.text: counter of the cost, of course

indicators.note: excitedly suggests agitation, so the letters of the words that follow are jumbled

explanation.surface: Mr Jones awaits something eagerly and spends without counting.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means that cost does not matter: a person who says it is no counter of cost.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says money spent is unimportant, so nobody tallies the price.

clue.text: The sort of sale that's all confusion

explanation.surface: A sale that is total chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: A JUMBLE sale is a British charity sale of second-hand odds and ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A rummage sale of donated goods takes this name, and a muddled mess is also one.

clue.text: Caught greatest boxer with firm making cotton?

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
Muhammad Ali called himself the greatest
Co is short for company, a firm

explanation.surface: The champion boxer signs with a firm producing cotton goods.
explanation.definitionFit: This plain woven fabric is made from cotton, hence the question mark for an example.

clue.text: Have one turn after another while on the way up

definitions.text: Have one turn after another while on the way up

parts.words: Have one turn after another while on the way up
parts.note: a winding ascent such as a twisting staircase or coil, one loop following the next as it climbs

explanation.definitionFit: A coil or helix rises in continuous loops, each turn following the last.

clue.text: Yes, Lamb's reorganised meeting

indicators.note: reorganised says the letters of the preceding words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Charles Lamb rearranges a gathering, and agrees to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering of people for a purpose is a meeting.

clue.text: The guard's last carriage in the forefront

explanation.surface: The guard rides in the final coach at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: A guard's VAN was the last carriage of a British train; 'van' is also short for vanguard, the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear railway wagon was the guard's, and the lead position of an army is its vanguard.

clue.text: Get wind of slight disturbance

explanation.surface: Hearing a rumour of a minor upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get wind of' means hear of; here 'wind' is a gentle wind, and a breeze is also British slang for a minor quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A light current of air is a gentle wind, and old slang uses the word for a small row.

clue.text: Battle of the century destroyed Clifton

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century

indicators.note: destroyed says the letters of the place name are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: The fight of the century wrecked Clifton, a suburb of Bristol.
explanation.definitionFit: A fight or war is a conflict.
